newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BAT holds ground on US tobacco deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BAT holds ground on US tobacco deal.

text.p: Britain's B.A.T Industries Plc said on Wednesday it would accept no fundamental changes to a proposed landmark settlement of legal claims between the U.S. tobacco industry and state attorneys.
"It's a package, in essence. Take it or leave it," B.A.T chief executive Martin Broughton told Reuters in an interview. "If you are looking for fundamental change, then no."

B.A.T, which earlier reported a five percent dip in first half pre-tax profits to 1.247 billion pounds, surprised investors by announcing it was keeping its half year and full year dividends unchanged because of the cost and uncertainty of the U.S. settlement.

"It's a case of short term pain for long term gain. The point of all this is that people will now be able to put a value on (key B.A.T subsidiary) Brown and Williamson..," said Michael Prideaux, head of group public affairs.
Brown & Williamson is the third largest cigarette maker in the United States with brands such as Kent, Lucky Strike and Kool.
News that the half-year payout was being held at 10p and the full year dividend at 16p sent shares sliding 23p to 517p in brisk trade by 1400 GMT.

But B.A.T reassured shareholders that the proposed U.S. resolution, under which U.S. tobacco companies would settle legal claims against them in return for payments of 230 billion pounds over 25 years, would not affect other countries.
"Shareholders may well be concerned about whether the proposed resolution will also affect other countries. We do not consider that it will," said chairman Lord Cairns in the results statement.
But analysts remained unappeased. They had forecast a dividend increase to between 10.7p and 10.8p per share at the half year stage and a five to eight percent rise in the final dividend.

"The maintenance of the dividend at 1996 levels shows some ill grace on the part of B.A.T management, which traditionally has had a commitment to a progressive dividend policy," said Tim Young, an analyst at SocGen.

Under the agreement between American tobacco companies and U.S. state attorneys sealed in June, the industry also accepted tougher regulation and advertising restrictions in return for immunity from most legal claims. The funds raised by the levy will be used to meet costs incurred for treating smoking related diseases.
But the company warned the U.S. against demanding restrictions on the sale of cigarettes outside the U.S.
"There is a tendency in the U.S. to seek to take extra-terrestrial jurisdiction. America should look after America and keep its nose out of anywhere else," chief executive Broughton stated.
If the settlement terms are approved by Congress, B.A.T will have to pay $1.7 billion upfront. The second payment into the fund falls due one year after enactment.
But Prideaux said the proposal was under attack from health groups and the timetable for enactment by Congress was slipping.
"We were hopeful it would be enacted by the end of this year but that is now looking less likely," he said, adding there were two important motives for not letting it slip too far.

"First, the $10 billion upfront payment is not payable until the proposals are enacted. Second, the first payment into the fund is not due until the end of the first full year following enactment. So the states which stand to get most of this money for their Medicaid programmes could be waiting until 1999."

Amid speculation that B.A.T might spin off its financial services business which includes Eagle Star in the UK, the group said there was little advantage in a straight demerger because of "financial inefficiencies" ahead of clarification on foreign income dividends (FIDS)
The government plans to abolish so-called FIDS, which allow companies to avoid paying tax in Britain on earnings already taxed abroad, from 1999.
B.A.T posted pretax profits of 1.247 billion pounds in the six months to June 30, down 64 million on the first half of 1996 -- mainly due to a 61 million pound impact of the strength of sterling.
Trading profit from tobacco rose six percent to 800 million pounds before exceptionals. But total cigarette volumes were flat at 340 billion pounds. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
